summary: Describes the External Data Representation standard, a common way to encode data so that different kinds of computers can exchange it. It is a draft standard and was replaced by RFC 4506.

eli5.summary: A common packing style so that any two computers open the same box and see the same things.

questions: what is xdr external data representation
why is xdr used in nfs and rpc
subtitle: A standard way for different computers to exchange data.

tldr.problem: Computers with different architectures (Intel, Sun, IBM) store integers, floating-point numbers, and other data in different byte orders and representations. When machines exchange data, they need a common format or translation step.
tldr.mechanism: XDR defines a standard encoding for all common data types (integers, floats, arrays, structures, strings). It specifies that all data aligns to 4-byte boundaries, uses big-endian byte order, and provides a language-like notation to describe data structures.
tldr.outcome: Any two computers can exchange data in XDR format and both will interpret it the same way, without requiring advance knowledge of each other's architecture.

today: RFC 1832 is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 4506, which makes minor clarifications but retains the same specification. XDR remains widely deployed in Network File System (NFS) implementations and Remote Procedure Call (RPC) systems. Modern protocols often use JSON or Protocol Buffers instead, but XDR continues to be a reference for machine-independent data encoding.

sections.title: Why We Need a Standard Format
sections.content:
Different computer architectures represent data differently. An Intel processor stores a 32-bit integer with the least significant byte first (little-endian), while a Motorola processor stores it with the most significant byte first (big-endian). Some systems align data on 2-byte boundaries, others on 4-byte or 8-byte boundaries. Without agreement, a number that means 5 on one machine might mean something completely different when read on another.

XDR (External Data Representation) solves this by defining a single, machine-independent encoding that any computer can produce and any other computer can read. It has been used in systems like Sun NFS (Network File System) and ONC RPC (Remote Procedure Call) since the 1980s. The encoding is simple enough that implementations are fast, yet complete enough to handle all common data types.
sections.eli5: When you mail a letter, you write the address the same way whether you use a pen from Japan or a pen from America. XDR is like a standard way of writing: every computer writes data the same way, so every other computer can read it.

sections.title: The 4-Byte Building Block
sections.content:
XDR's fundamental rule is that all data is aligned to 4-byte (32-bit) boundaries. Any piece of data that takes fewer than 4 bytes is padded with zero bytes to reach the next multiple of 4. For example, a 1-byte boolean becomes 4 bytes (one data byte plus three zero-padding bytes), a 2-byte value becomes 4 bytes, and an 8-byte number stays 8 bytes (a multiple of 4).

This 4-byte block size represents a compromise: it is large enough to handle alignment requirements on most common architectures (Intel x86, SPARC, PowerPC), yet small enough to keep encoded data reasonably compact. The byte order within blocks is always big-endian (most significant byte first), regardless of the source machine's native order.
sections.eli5: Every data chunk must be a multiple of 4 bytes. If you have just 1 byte, you add 3 zero-padding bytes. If you have 5 bytes, you add 3 more to get to 8.

sections.title: Standard Data Types
sections.content:
XDR defines concrete encodings for all basic types. Integers and unsigned integers are 32-bit two's complement numbers in big-endian byte order. Booleans are encoded as integers (0=FALSE, 1=TRUE). Hyper integers are 64-bit two's complement numbers. Floating-point numbers (32-bit) and double-precision numbers (64-bit) use IEEE 754 standard encoding. XDR also defines opaque data (raw bytes), strings (length-prefixed ASCII), fixed-length arrays, variable-length arrays (with a count prefix), structures (components in order), and discriminated unions (a tag value determines which field is present).

Variable-length data is preceded by a 32-bit count indicating the number of bytes or elements that follow. Optional fields are encoded as a boolean flag followed by the data if the flag is true.
sections.eli5: XDR says: here's how to encode an integer (4 bytes, big-endian), here's how to encode a string (4-byte length, then the characters, padded to 4 bytes), and here's how to encode a structure (each field one after another).

sections.title: The XDR Language Notation
sections.content:
XDR provides a C-like language for describing data structures. The language is not executable code; it is purely for documentation and specification. Using this language, a protocol designer can precisely describe what data will be exchanged. For example, a simple structure might be declared as:

struct filetype { string filename<255>; unsigned int filesize; opaque data<65535>; };

This declares a structure with three fields: a string (up to 255 bytes), an unsigned integer, and opaque data (up to 65535 bytes). The language supports type definitions (typedef), named constants (const), enumerated types, nested structures, and unions. The syntax is similar to C, making it familiar to programmers, yet it is purely declarative—a protocol specification, not executable code.
sections.eli5: XDR has a notation that looks like C. You say int age; or string name<100>; to describe what will be sent. It's like a blueprint that says what the data will look like.

sections.title: Design Decisions and Trade-offs
sections.content:
XDR's design reflects deliberate trade-offs. The RFC uses implicit typing (the receiver knows what type to expect from the protocol specification) rather than explicit type tags, reducing overhead and keeping encoded data compact. It uses big-endian byte order for consistency, even though this slightly disadvantages little-endian machines like the VAX which must convert. It uses 4-byte blocks as a compromise between supporting many architectures and keeping data size reasonable.

XDR does not include explicit support for bit fields or bitmaps, since the standard is byte-oriented. Padding with zeros rather than random bytes ensures that the same data encodes identically on all machines, allowing checksums to be computed over XDR-encoded data with portable results. These choices make XDR simple, fast to implement, and suitable for use in network protocols like NFS and RPC.
sections.eli5: XDR's creators made choices: big-endian byte order for everyone (fair to nobody, but consistent), 4-byte blocks (works on most machines), and no type tags in the data (you must know what to expect). These choices keep the format simple and the encoding fast.
